title: CMake, Libraries and Package Managers
summary: Real projects have many files and use third-party libraries. **CMake** describes *what* to build portably and generates the build files for your tools. Libraries are **static** (copied into your executable) or **dynamic** (loaded while running). **vcpkg** and **Conan** download libraries for you.
markdown:
## Beyond a single program Xenon compiles your files for you. A real project needs a description of what to build: which source files form which programs and libraries, with which settings, depending on which outside code. This lesson is about that machinery. It cannot be run inside Xenon, but you will need it for your first project outside. ## Static and dynamic libraries A **library** is compiled code packaged for reuse. ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph Static["Static library (.lib, .a)"] direction LR S1["mathlib.lib"] -->|"copied in at LINK time"| S2["game.exe
larger, self-contained"] end subgraph Dynamic["Dynamic library (.dll, .so)"] direction LR D1["game.exe
smaller"] -->|"loaded at RUN time"| D2["mathlib.dll
must be present"] end ``` | | Static | Dynamic | |---|---|---| | When it is joined to your program | By the linker | When the program starts | | Executable size | Larger | Smaller | | What you distribute | One file | The executable and the library file | | Update the library without rebuilding | No | Yes | | Shared in memory between programs | No | Yes | ### Using a library takes three things | What | Who needs it | Why | |---|---|---| | The **headers** | The compiler | To know what the library declares | | The **library file** | The linker | To resolve the calls | | The **dynamic library**, if there is one | The running program | It must be found beside the executable or on the system path | Missing headers give compile errors. A missing library file gives "unresolved external symbol". A missing DLL gives an error when the program starts. Knowing which stage failed tells you which of the three is wrong ([[1.08 Multiple Files and Headers]]). ## CMake CMake does not compile anything. It reads a description of your project and **generates** build files for whatever tool you use: a Visual Studio solution, Makefiles or Ninja files. ``` my_game/ ├── CMakeLists.txt ├── src/ │ ├── main.cpp │ └── game/ │ ├── Player.h │ └── Player.cpp └── tests/ └── test_player.cpp ``` ### CMakeLists.txt ```cmake cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.25) project(MyGame VERSION 1.0 LANGUAGES CXX) set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 20) set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD_REQUIRED ON) set(CMAKE_CXX_EXTENSIONS OFF) # A library holding the game logic add_library(game_core src/game/Player.cpp) target_include_directories(game_core PUBLIC src) if (MSVC) target_compile_options(game_core PRIVATE /W4 /permissive-) else() target_compile_options(game_core PRIVATE -Wall -Wextra -Wconversion -pedantic) endif() # The program add_executable(my_game src/main.cpp) target_link_libraries(my_game PRIVATE game_core) ``` ### Building ```bash cmake -S . -B build ``` ```bash cmake --build build --config Release ``` ```mermaid flowchart LR CM["CMakeLists.txt"] -->|"configure:
cmake -S . -B build"| G["build/
generated build files"] G -->|"build:
cmake --build build"| E["my_game.exe"] ``` Everything generated goes into `build/`, separate from your sources. Visual Studio, CLion and VS Code all open a CMake project directly. ### Targets Modern CMake is organised around **targets**: a library or an executable, together with what it needs. | Command | Does | |---|---| | `add_executable(name sources...)` | Defines a program | | `add_library(name sources...)` | Defines a library | | `target_include_directories(...)` | Says where a target's headers are | | `target_compile_options(...)` | Adds compiler flags for a target | | `target_link_libraries(a PRIVATE b)` | Makes `a` use `b` | Each property carries a visibility keyword that says who it applies to. | Keyword | Applies to | |---|---| | `PRIVATE` | This target only | | `PUBLIC` | This target **and** everything that links to it | | `INTERFACE` | Only the things that link to it (as for a header-only library) | `game_core`'s include directory is `PUBLIC`, so `my_game` receives it automatically by linking to `game_core`. Putting the logic in a library, with a thin executable on top, also lets a test program link the same library. ## Getting third-party libraries ### FetchContent Built into CMake: it downloads and builds a dependency as part of your project. ```cmake include(FetchContent) FetchContent_Declare(fmt GIT_REPOSITORY https://github.com/fmtlib/fmt.git GIT_TAG 11.0.2) FetchContent_MakeAvailable(fmt) target_link_libraries(my_game PRIVATE fmt::fmt) ``` ### vcpkg A **package manager** downloads, builds and caches libraries, so each project only lists what it needs. vcpkg is Microsoft's; it works on every platform. ```bash vcpkg new --application ``` ```bash vcpkg add port raylib nlohmann-json ``` ```cmake find_package(raylib CONFIG REQUIRED) target_link_libraries(my_game PRIVATE raylib) ``` Pass vcpkg's toolchain file when configuring, and `find_package` locates what it installed. **Conan** is a widely used alternative with the same purpose. | Approach | Good for | |---|---| | FetchContent | A few small dependencies; nothing extra to install | | vcpkg or Conan | Many or large dependencies; builds are cached and shared across projects | ## Libraries worth knowing | Area | Libraries | |---|---| | Formatting and logging | {fmt}, spdlog | | JSON | nlohmann/json, simdjson | | Testing | GoogleTest, Catch2, doctest | | 2D games and graphics | raylib, SFML, SDL | | 3D graphics | OpenGL with GLFW and glm; Vulkan | | User interfaces | Dear ImGui, Qt | | Networking | Asio, cpr | | Mathematics | Eigen, glm | | Much else | Boost | ## Check yourself ```quiz ? What does `target_link_libraries(app PRIVATE core)` do? - It makes `core` part of `app`'s public interface for everything that links `app` + It links `core` into `app` and gives `app` the `PUBLIC` properties of `core`, without passing them on - It copies the source files of `core` into `app` - It builds `core` only in Debug builds > `PRIVATE` means `app` uses `core` internally. Anything linking to `app` does not inherit `core`'s requirements. ? Which kind of library needs a file distributed with the executable? - A static library + A dynamic library - A header-only library - Every kind of library > A static library is copied into the executable while linking. A dynamic library (`.dll`, `.so`) is loaded when the program starts. ? Does CMake compile your code? - Yes, it is a compiler + No, it generates build files for other tools - Only for C files, not for C++ - Only when using a package manager > CMake describes the project and generates, for example, Ninja files or a Visual Studio solution. Those then run the compiler. ? The program builds but fails on start-up saying a DLL is missing. Which of the three requirements failed? - The compile-time one: the header was not found - The link-time one: the import library was not linked + The run-time one: the DLL is not where it can be found > It built, so compiling and linking succeeded. Only the run-time search for the DLL failed. ```
ideas:
These need a compiler and CMake installed on your own machine.
1. Convert a multi-file project into CMake, with a `core` library and an `app` executable.
2. Add {fmt} with FetchContent and use it for output.
3. Build a maths module as a static library and as a shared library, and compare the executable sizes.

cards.a:
It links `core` into `app` and gives `app` the `PUBLIC` properties of `core`, without passing them on

`PRIVATE` means `app` uses `core` internally. Anything linking to `app` does not inherit `core`'s requirements.

cards.q: Which kind of library needs a file distributed with the executable?
cards.a:
A dynamic library

A static library is copied into the executable while linking. A dynamic library (`.dll`, `.so`) is loaded when the program starts.

No, it generates build files for other tools

CMake describes the project and generates, for example, Ninja files or a Visual Studio solution. Those then run the compiler.

cards.q: The program builds but fails on start-up saying a DLL is missing. Which of the three requirements failed?
cards.a:
The run-time one: the DLL is not where it can be found

It built, so compiling and linking succeeded. Only the run-time search for the DLL failed.
